transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Um, hi. Well, I guess I'm here because... work has just been really hard lately. I do hair, and my hands literally feel like they’re moving through glue. Like, even just sectioning hair or mixing the color bowls takes me forever now. We use this specific brand of color at my salon which usually mixes really easy, not like the cheap stuff I had to use back in cosmetology school. My instructor back then, Ms. Davis, she was so strict about how we mixed it. She actually had this tiny little dog she would bring into the back office... a Pomeranian, I think? It barked at absolutely everyone who walked by the breakroom. But um... yeah, people at the salon have started noticing I’m just way slower than I used to be. My clients, my manager... everybody sees it. So I guess that's why I'm here.
Are you experiencing any difficulties or slowness in activities outside of work?

I mean, I guess at home too, but like I was just saying, it's mainly at the salon where it's a huge problem. My hands just feel like they’re moving through glue, you know? Even just sectioning the hair or mixing the color takes me forever now. I used to be so fast. My friend Sarah—she works at the lash studio next door—she is incredibly fast. She can do a full volume lash set in like 45 minutes. I tried getting lash extensions from her once, but the adhesive she used made my eyes water so bad. I guess I'm allergic to whatever chemical is in it. My eyes were puffy for like two whole days, I looked absolutely ridiculous. I actually had to wear my giant sunglasses inside the grocery store, which probably made me look like I was trying to be famous or something. 

But um... wait, what did you ask me? Oh, right, outside of work. Yeah, I don't know, it's just like I said, people have started noticing I’m just way slower than I used to be, no matter what I'm doing.
Do you feel like your hands are physically weak or do you just have trouble coordinating their movements

Um, no, they're not weak, I don't think. It's not like I can't lift things. It's just... like I said, it really just feels like my hands are moving through glue at work. Like even sectioning hair or mixing color takes me forever now. Mixing color used to be my favorite part, honestly. You get to be so creative with it. I had this one client, Jessica, who wanted this crazy vivid purple balayage, and we had to lift her hair from like a level three dark brown all the way to a nine before we could even deposit the purple. It took like six hours. We ended up ordering pizza halfway through because we were both starving. It was from that place down the street, Mario's? They have the best garlic knots, but they always forget the marinara sauce. It drives my manager crazy when they forget the sauce. 

But yeah... it's not weakness. It's just that I'm so much slower than I used to be, and people have started noticing.
Do you ever find yourself having trouble starting a task, even when you want to do it?

Um, yeah, I guess so. Like... I just don't have that spark in me anymore to start things. I used to be so outgoing, you know? I would chat with all my clients, and I'd even help the newer stylists when they were struggling with a tricky cut or a difficult toner formulation. Toner can be so tricky because if you leave an ash toner on porous hair for even a minute too long, it grabs so fast and turns everything muddy or green. I had to fix this girl's hair once who tried to tone her own highlights at home with a box dye, and it was a complete disaster. She was crying in my chair. We had to do a soap cap to strip it out, which is basically just mixing bleach with clarifying shampoo. Clarifying shampoo always makes my hands so dry, though. I have to use this heavy shea butter lotion every night or my knuckles crack. 

But um... what was I saying? Oh, right. Yeah, I just don't have that energy anymore. I used to go hiking with my friends all the time on my days off, but now I just mostly keep my head down at the salon and try to avoid people. It's just really hard to get myself to do anything.
Do you feel like you're having trouble finding the right words when you're talking?

Um, no, I don't think so. I mean, I feel like I can talk fine. I just... I talk a lot, I guess. My mom always said I could talk to a brick wall if you let me. She used to get so mad when I was little because I would just talk and talk during church. We went to this really old Catholic church with those beautiful stained glass windows, you know the ones? The light would come through them in the morning and make all these pretty colors on the pews. I actually tried to dye a client's hair once to look like stained glass. We did block coloring with deep blues and magentas and emerald greens. It looked amazing, but she used hot water when she washed it the first time, and all the colors bled together into this weird, muddy brown. I felt so bad, but I told her to use cold water! Cold water is so important for fashion colors. It's miserable in the winter, though, taking a freezing cold shower just to keep your hair pink. 

But um... yeah, no, I don't have trouble finding words. I just... I just don't really want to talk to people as much as I used to.
Do you feel anxious or nervous, either at work or in your daily life?

Um, not really anxious, no. Just... more like I don't care about anything anymore. It's not nervousness, it's just this heavy feeling. Like, I used to get nervous before a big color correction, you know? Like when someone comes in with banded hair from using three different box dyes over the last year. Those are so stressful because you never know what's under there until the lightener hits it. I had this one girl who swore she hadn't colored her hair in two years, but as soon as the bleach went on, this bright pink ring showed up right in the middle of the hair shaft. Splat hair dye, I swear, it never comes out. It literally stains the cuticle. We had to pivot and do a root melt into a rose gold just to hide it. Rose gold was so popular a few years ago, everybody wanted it. We used to mix this custom formula with a little bit of copper and a tiny drop of pink. It faded so fast, though. That's the thing with those pastel tones, they look gorgeous for like two washes and then you're just left with blonde. 

But um... yeah, no. Not anxious. Just... empty, I guess. I just don't have the energy to even get nervous anymore.
Do you have trouble with coordination or movement in your daily activities outside of the salon?

Um, well... I guess I do feel a little different with how I move. It's not like I'm tripping over things or anything, but... my hands just feel like they're moving through glue. Especially at work. Like, even just sectioning hair or mixing color, it takes me forever now. People have definitely started noticing that I'm just slower than I used to be. My manager actually pulled me aside the other day to ask if I was feeling okay because my blowout times have doubled. Blowouts are so exhausting anyway, especially if someone has really thick, coarse hair. You have to use so much tension with the round brush to get it smooth, and your shoulders just ache by the end of the day. I have this one client, she has the most beautiful, thick Dominican hair, but it takes me a solid hour just to blow it out. We usually use this amazing smoothing serum that smells like coconuts and argan oil. Argan oil is literally liquid gold, I put it on everything. I even use it on my cuticles when they get dry from the clarifying shampoo. 

But um... yeah, my hands just feel so heavy and slow. Everything just feels like it takes so much effort now.
Have you been having any trouble sleeping lately?

Um, no, not really. I mean, I sleep okay, I guess. I just... I sleep a lot, honestly. When I'm not at the salon, I'm usually just in bed. It's so hard to get up in the mornings, especially when it's cold out. My bedroom gets so drafty because the windows in my apartment are super old. They're those old wooden sash windows, and the landlord refuses to fix them. I tried putting that plastic shrink wrap stuff over them last winter? You know, the kind you have to use a blow dryer to seal? It actually works really well, but it looks so tacky. I brought my professional Dyson blow dryer home from work to do it because it gets so much hotter than a regular one. That blow dryer is amazing, it cut my drying time in half at the salon. It's so lightweight, too, which is great because my wrists used to kill me. Carpal tunnel is like the number one thing stylists get, honestly. That and bad backs from standing all day. You really have to wear good shoes. I bought these ugly orthotic clogs that look terrible, but they save my feet. 

But um... yeah, no trouble sleeping. I just... I just sleep all the time because I don't really want to be awake.
Do you feel like you've lost interest in activities you used to enjoy?

Um, yeah, I guess so. I mean, I used to love chatting with my clients, you know? Like, we'd talk about everything, and I'd even help the newer stylists out when they got stuck on a color formulation. And on my days off, I'd go hiking with my friends all the time. There's this really great trail just outside the city that goes up to this waterfall. It's so pretty in the fall when the leaves change. I used to try to match hair colors to the autumn leaves—like those rich coppers and deep auburns. Auburn is so tricky, though, because if you don't formulate right, it just looks muddy or way too red. You have to balance the warmth with a little bit of brown, or else it just looks unnatural. I had a client who wanted this perfect copper penny color, and it took three appointments to get it right because her hair was so porous from swimming. Chlorine just eats color, it's the worst. You have to use a clarifying shampoo and then a really intense deep conditioner before you even think about putting color over chlorine damage. We have this one mask at the salon that has keratin in it, and it literally saves people's hair. 

But... yeah. Now I mostly just keep my head down at work. I try to avoid people, honestly. I just don't have that spark in me anymore to even talk or do any of those things.
Do you still enjoy doing your hair work when you're not at the salon, like practicing new techniques or trying out different styles on yourself or friends?

Um, no, not really. I don't really do anything with hair when I'm not at the salon anymore. I used to practice braiding on my roommate, actually. She has this really long, fine hair that just slips right out of a braid if you don't use the right products. We used to sit in the living room and watch reality TV while I tried out all these intricate styles I'd see on Instagram. Instagram is so crazy now with all these hair tutorials, they make it look so easy but they speed up the video and edit out all the hard parts. Like, you can't just do a five-strand Dutch braid in thirty seconds, it's impossible. Plus, you have to use so much texturizing spray to get it to look thick and messy like they do online. I love this one sea salt spray we sell at the salon, it smells exactly like the beach. My roommate loved it too, she'd always steal it from my room. We used to go to the beach a lot before she moved out. She got this job in marketing and had to move closer to downtown, so now I just live by myself. It's kind of lonely, but at least I don't have to share a bathroom anymore. Sharing a bathroom with another girl is a nightmare when you both have a million hair products. 

But um... yeah, no, I don't really practice or do anything like that anymore. I just don't have the energy for it.
Do you feel guilty about anything?

Um, yeah. I guess I do. I just... I keep thinking I'm a burden on everyone, you know? Like I deserve what's happening to me because I couldn't keep my money or my job or even just basic salon responsibilities together. It's so embarrassing when you mess up at the salon because everyone sees it. Like, the mirrors are everywhere, so you can literally watch your client's face drop if you cut their bangs too short. Bangs are the worst. People always come in with these pictures of curtain bangs, but they don't realize you have to style them every single day or they just lay flat on your forehead and look greasy. You have to use a round brush and blow them away from your face, and then hit them with the cool shot button on the dryer to set the shape. The cool shot is so important, but nobody ever uses it at home. They just blast their hair with heat until it's fried. I had this one client who flat-ironed her hair every day on the highest setting without heat protectant, and her ends were literally breaking off in my hands. It was so sad. I tried to sell her this thermal protectant spray we have, but it's like thirty dollars and people get so mad about salon prices. But the drugstore stuff just has so much alcohol in it, it dries your hair out even more.

But um... yeah. I just feel like I'm dragging everyone down. I can't even do the basics right anymore.
Do you still find pleasure in the things you used to enjoy?

Um, no... not really. I think I already mentioned that, but yeah, I just don't have that spark in me anymore. Like, I used to love chatting with my clients and helping the newer stylists mix their colors, and I'd go hiking with my friends on the weekends. But now I just mostly keep my head down and avoid people. It's just too much. Even being in the breakroom is exhausting because everyone is always gossiping about who left their station a mess or who took someone else's foil. Foil is actually super expensive, especially the pre-cut pop-up ones with the embossed texture. They grip the hair so much better than the smooth ones, so the lightener doesn't bleed and leave those horrible cheetah spots at the root. Color correction for cheetah spots is a nightmare. You have to go in with a tiny brush and tap a shadow root over every single spot, and it takes hours. Clients get so impatient sitting in the chair for that long, and their scalps get sensitive from all the processing. I always try to put a little Sweet'n Low in the bleach to stop the burning—it's this old school trick my cosmetology teacher taught me. She was this amazing lady who used to do hair for theater productions in the 80s, so she knew all these weird hacks. 

But um... yeah. I don't really find pleasure in any of it anymore. I just avoid everyone.
Do you feel sad most of the time?

Yeah, I do. Most days I just wake up with this really heavy, flat sadness right in my chest. It just feels like there's no point in trying to build the life I was planning, you know? Like, I was planning to open my own studio eventually. You know those salon suites you can rent? They're getting super popular right now because you get your own little room with a chair and a washbowl, and you can decorate it however you want. I wanted to paint mine this really soft sage green and have lots of hanging plants. Pothos plants are the best for salons because they don't need a lot of natural light, and the humidity from the steamers actually helps them grow. We use these ozone steamers for deep conditioning treatments, especially for clients with low porosity hair. Low porosity hair is so stubborn, the cuticle is basically sealed shut so moisture just sits on top of the strand instead of absorbing. You have to use heat to lift the cuticle, otherwise, you're just wasting product. And professional deep conditioners are not cheap. I bought this huge tub of a bond-building mask for the backbar once and someone left the lid off and it dried out. I was so mad. The bond builders are amazing though, they literally rebuild the disulfide bonds in the hair after you bleach it. It's basically science. I loved learning the chemistry part of cosmetology school, like mixing the developers and understanding the pH scale of different color lines. 

But um... yeah. Sorry, what was the question? Oh, feeling sad. Yeah, it's just that heavy, flat feeling every morning.
Do you still enjoy doing anything outside of work?

Um, no, not really. I mean, I used to do this volunteer thing at the senior center, giving haircuts to the residents, but I just... I stopped showing up for it. I couldn't handle it anymore. And I've pretty much pulled away from all my friends, too. I just don't have the energy to pretend I'm okay. It's just like at work... I've completely lost the trust of my manager and my clients. I'm making all these mistakes with just basic salon routines, and I'm working so slowly. I keep canceling appointments that I used to handle with no problem. It's embarrassing. 

Like, the other day I was doing a basic root touch-up, which is literally cosmetology 101. You just section the hair into four quadrants—you always start at the nape of the neck because that hair is the strongest and takes the longest to process. If you start at the front hairline, those fine baby hairs will process way too fast and you'll get a hot root. Hot roots are the worst. It's when the root is visibly lighter or warmer than the rest of the hair because the heat from the scalp speeds up the chemical reaction. You have to be so careful with the developer volume. Most people think you need 30 or 40 volume to get a good lift, but honestly, 20 volume is usually plenty if you just give it enough time and maybe use a little heat, but not too much heat or you'll melt the hair. I had a client once who tried to bleach her own hair at home with 40 volume and a plastic grocery bag over her head, and her hair literally turned into chewing gum. It was so gummy and stretchy, it's called a loss of elasticity. When hair loses its elasticity, you can't even brush it when it's wet or it just snaps off. You have to do all these protein treatments, but protein can actually make the hair brittle if you use too much of it. It's a really delicate balance between moisture and protein.

But um... yeah. I don't really do anything outside of work anymore. I just cancel everything and stay away from people.
Do you still enjoy any small pleasures in life, like eating your favorite food or taking a warm bath?

Um, no, not really. Even eating... I don't know, it's just a chore now. I’ve actually been skipping meals without really meaning to. Like, I'll get to the end of the day and realize all I've had is coffee and maybe a few bites of a protein bar. My clothes have definitely gotten looser. But honestly, eating at the salon is always a disaster anyway. You never really get a lunch break. You're always double-booking, so while one client's color is processing, you're cutting someone else's hair. And if you do try to eat in the back room, it always smells like perm solution or Barbicide. Barbicide is that blue liquid we use to disinfect our combs and shears. You have to completely submerge the tools for at least ten minutes, but if you leave them in too long, it can actually rust the metal. Good shears are an investment, like, a really good pair of Japanese steel shears can cost over a thousand dollars. The steel is so much harder, so the blade stays sharp longer, which is super important for slide cutting. If your shears are dull, it pushes the hair instead of slicing it, and you get these really blunt, choppy layers instead of a soft blend. Blending is everything, especially with men's fades. You have to use the clippers with the guards in a specific order, like starting with a two and blending down to a zero, using the lever to open and close the blade. If you don't flick your wrist just right at the parietal ridge, you leave this harsh line of weight that looks terrible. 

But um... what were you asking? Oh, food and baths. Yeah, I just forget to eat mostly. I don't really care about my favorite foods anymore.
Have you ever thought about hurting yourself?

Um... I don't really have a plan to hurt myself or anything like that. But I do get these thoughts sometimes, like... maybe it would just be easier if I didn't wake up. Waking up is just so exhausting anyway, especially when I used to have to do the opening shifts at the salon. 

Opening shifts are the worst because you have to get there an hour early just to turn on the wax pots. Hard wax takes literally forever to melt down to the right consistency. It has to look like thick honey. If it's too runny, it's way too hot and you'll burn the client, but if it's too thick, it won't spread evenly. Hard wax is so much better for facial waxing, though, because it only adheres to the hair, not the skin. Soft wax—the kind where you use the little muslin strips—can actually lift a whole layer of skin if you pull it up instead of parallel, or if the client is using retinol at home. Retinol speeds up cell turnover, so the top layer of skin is super thin and fragile. You always have to do a consultation and ask about their skincare routine, but clients lie all the time because they just want their eyebrows done. Eyebrow mapping is honestly an art form. You use this string covered in white charcoal and map out the golden ratio on their face. You measure from the dimple of the nose to find the front of the brow, and then angle it right through the pupil to find the highest point of the arch. If you bring the tail down too far, it drags the whole face down and makes the person look sad... 

But um... sorry. What were we talking about? Oh, right. Yeah, no plan to hurt myself. I just... I just think it would be easier if I didn't wake up and nobody had to deal with me anymore.
Do you feel like you no longer enjoy or find pleasure in things that you used to like?

Um... yeah, I really don't. I used to love chatting with my clients, you know? And I'd always help the newer stylists figure things out on the floor. I even used to go hiking with my friends on the weekends. But now I just... I keep my head down and avoid people. I just don't have that spark in me anymore. 

It's kind of like when you're trying to do a balayage on someone who has box dye in their hair. Box dye is a nightmare because it has metallic salts in it, and when you put lightener over it, it literally smokes. Like, the hair gets so hot it can burn your hand through the foil. Balayage is supposed to look really natural and sun-kissed, like you just spent a month at the beach. You hand-paint the lightener on, usually in a V-shape or a W-shape on the hair section, so the root stays dark and it blends seamlessly down to the ends. You have to have the right tension on the hair when you're painting, or the brush skips and you get these weird cheetah spots. And you always have to use a clay-based lightener for balayage because it forms a hard shell on the outside but stays moist on the inside, so it doesn't bleed onto the hair underneath it. If you use regular foil lightener without foils, it just swells and makes a huge mess. Plus, you have to tone it afterward anyway. Toners are demi-permanent, so they only deposit color, they don't lift. You use them to cancel out unwanted warmth, like using a violet toner to cancel out yellow, or a blue toner to cancel out orange. It's just basic color theory, right on the color wheel. If you put an ash toner on pale yellow hair, sometimes it grabs too much and turns gray or green, which is why you have to watch it process at the bowl. You can't just walk away.

But um... yeah, no spark anymore. I just avoid everyone now.
Have you ever thought about how you would hurt yourself if you were to act on those thoughts about not waking up?

Um, no, I... like I said, I don't have a plan or anything. I don't sit around thinking about how I'd do it. It's just more like... I just wish I wouldn't wake up. Like my body would just stop on its own and nobody would have to deal with me anymore. Because dealing with people is just... it's a lot. 

It reminds me of when clients come in wanting a color correction and they expect it to be done in two hours. Color corrections are literally a full-day process. You have to strip out whatever they did to it at home, which usually involves color removers that smell like rotten eggs. The sulfur in them shrinks the artificial color molecules so you can wash them out, but if you don't rinse for at least twenty minutes, the molecules just expand again as soon as you put peroxide on the hair. And then you have to do a strand test to see what you're even working with, because the hair underneath could be completely compromised. If the hair feels gummy or stretches like a rubber band when it's wet, that means the disulfide bonds are broken and you can't put any more lightener on it or it will literally melt off in your hands. That's why Olaplex was such a big deal when it came out. It actually rebuilds those broken bonds. You mix step one right into the lightener, and then step two is a standalone treatment at the bowl. But it's not a magic wand, you know? You still have to manage their expectations. Like, no, you cannot go from black box dye to platinum blonde in one session. It's a journey. 

But um... what did you ask me? Oh, right. No, no plan to hurt myself. Just... just wishing I wouldn't wake up.
Have you thought about a specific way you would hurt yourself if you were to act on those thoughts about not waking up?

Um, I think you already asked me that, right? I really don't have a specific way or a plan or anything. I just... I get these thoughts that it would be so much easier if I just didn't wake up. Like, if I just faded out and nobody had to deal with me anymore. 

Dealing with people is just so draining. It's kind of like when you have a client who insists on getting a perm even though their hair is heavily highlighted. You just know it's a disaster waiting to happen. Perm solution breaks down the structural bonds of the hair so you can reshape it around the rods, but if the hair is already compromised from bleach, the perm solution will just fry it. You have to use an acid perm instead of an alkaline perm because it's gentler, but even then, it's so risky. And rolling the hair is so tedious. You have to use end papers so the tips of the hair don't get fishhooked, which is when they bend back on themselves and look frizzy forever. You have to keep the tension perfectly even across the whole rod, or the curl pattern will be completely inconsistent. And the smell of the thioglycolic acid is just... it lingers in your nose all day. You have to rinse it for a solid five minutes before you even apply the neutralizer, which rebonds the hair into the new shape. If you don't neutralize properly, the curl just falls right out the second they wash it at home. And you always have to tell them not to wash it for 48 hours, like in Legally Blonde. 

But yeah... sorry, I'm doing it again. Like I said, no plan. I just... I just don't want to wake up sometimes.
Have you thought about a specific way you would end your life if you were to act on those thoughts?

Um, I... I feel like we just talked about this. You keep asking me the same thing. I don't have a plan. I don't know how else to say it. I don't sit there thinking about how to end my life or what I would use. I just... I get these thoughts that it would be so much easier if I just didn't wake up tomorrow. Just... gone, you know? And then nobody would have to deal with me or worry about me anymore. 

Worrying about people is exhausting. It's like when clients come in and they're panicking because they tried to cut their own bangs at home. It's always a disaster. They watch one TikTok tutorial and think they can just take kitchen scissors and chop straight across. But they don't realize you have to account for cowlicks and how the hair jumps up when it dries. If you cut it wet, it's going to shrink at least half an inch, sometimes more if they have a wave pattern. You have to section out a perfect triangle from the high point of the head to the outer corners of the eyes. If you go too wide, you end up with a mullet situation, and if you go too deep, the bangs are way too thick and heavy. And you never cut straight across. You have to point-cut into the ends to give it texture and movement, otherwise it just looks like a blunt curtain sitting on their forehead. And fixing it is so hard because you can't add hair back. You just have to try and blend it into face-framing layers and pray it grows out fast. I always tell them to just come in for a bang trim, it takes like five minutes and most salons do it for free between appointments. 

But um... yeah. I don't have a plan. Just... just the thoughts about not waking up.

You just know it's a disaster waiting to happen. Perm solution breaks down the structural bonds of the hair so you can reshape it around the rods, but if the hair is already compromised from bleach, the perm solution will just fry it. You have to use an acid perm instead of an alkaline perm because it's gentler, but even then, it's so risky. And rolling the hair is so tedious. You have to use end papers so the tips of the hair don't get fishhooked, which is when they bend back on themselves and look frizzy forever. You have to keep the tension perfectly even across the whole rod, or the curl pattern will be completely inconsistent. And the smell of the thioglycolic acid is just... it lingers in your nose all day. You have to rinse it for a solid five minutes before you even apply the neutralizer, which rebonds the hair into the new shape. If you don't neutralize properly, the curl just falls right out the second they wash it at home. And you always have to tell them not to wash it for 48 hours, like in Legally Blonde. 

But yeah... sorry, I'm doing it again. Like I said, no plan. I just... I just don't want to wake up sometimes.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of suicidal intent with a plan
doctor.question: Have you thought about a specific way you would end your life if you were to act on those thoughts?

target_item.name: Death_Suicide
target_item.manifestation: I don’t have a plan to hurt myself, but I get thoughts like it would be easier if I just didn’t wake up and nobody had to deal with me anymore.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking again about specific plans or methods for ending my life, which directly relates to suicidal ideation.

patient.answer:
Um, I... I feel like we just talked about this. You keep asking me the same thing. I don't have a plan. I don't know how else to say it. I don't sit there thinking about how to end my life or what I would use. I just... I get these thoughts that it would be so much easier if I just didn't wake up tomorrow. Just... gone, you know? And then nobody would have to deal with me or worry about me anymore. 

Worrying about people is exhausting. It's like when clients come in and they're panicking because they tried to cut their own bangs at home. It's always a disaster. They watch one TikTok tutorial and think they can just take kitchen scissors and chop straight across. But they don't realize you have to account for cowlicks and how the hair jumps up when it dries. If you cut it wet, it's going to shrink at least half an inch, sometimes more if they have a wave pattern. You have to section out a perfect triangle from the high point of the head to the outer corners of the eyes. If you go too wide, you end up with a mullet situation, and if you go too deep, the bangs are way too thick and heavy. And you never cut straight across. You have to point-cut into the ends to give it texture and movement, otherwise it just looks like a blunt curtain sitting on their forehead. And fixing it is so hard because you can't add hair back. You just have to try and blend it into face-framing layers and pray it grows out fast. I always tell them to just come in for a bang trim, it takes like five minutes and most salons do it for free between appointments. 

But um... yeah. I don't have a plan. Just... just the thoughts about not waking up.
